title: sse-partial-frame-hang-debug-scratchpad
content:
High-level summary:

Observed a recurrent class of streaming failures where the server starts an SSE/text-event-stream stream, emits a few well-formed chunks, then appears to 'hang' mid-response. Client receives initial events, then nothing for 10s+ while connection stays ESTABLISHED. No obvious server-side crash or OOM. Repro is intermittent but deterministic under certain load and network conditions.

Key observations (fresh angles):
- The stall often occurs after ~6–12 KB of data has been sent for a single request (not related to token limits).
- tcpdump shows TCP packets leaving server for the first NKB; then outgoing packets stop even though server process is inside the write path.
- Client-side TCP receive window is not saturated; the server's send buffer appears to fill.
- Happens more frequently over TLS (ALPN h2 and HTTP/1.1 both observed) and less often on plaintext in lab.
- When reproducing through nginx as a reverse proxy, adding "X-Accel-Buffering: no" reduces occurrence but does not eliminate it.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) TLS record / kernel coalescing interaction + Nagle causes partial record to be buffered, then a small remaining write waits for ACKs which are delayed because the client-side event loop isn't reading fast enough (or a proxy is holding).
2) The serving runtime's SSE encoder occasionally emits a zero-length chunk or a malformed chunk-size line that confuses intermediary HTTP/1.1 chunk parsers leading to internal buffering in the proxy until a timeout (rare but seen in earlier traces).
3) Go runtime (or underlying C library path) intermittently sets TCP_CORK/TCP_NODELAY or uses sendfile path that leaves a TLS record incomplete when combined with crypto.Write() buffering — more visible over TLS.
4) Continuous batching & KV-cache flushing in runtime can block the response goroutine if code path tries to flush model tokens to disk / metric sinks synchronously on rare branches.

Commands & quick repros I used (work on mac/linux):

1) Raw curl client to observe streaming and timing:

curl -v -N --no-buffer "https://local-rw:8443/v1/streams?model=test-sse"

Notes: -N/--no-buffer and --no-keepalive helpful; use --raw on older curl builds to avoid chunk decoding. I usually run with -v to see headers and timings.

2) Node fetch streaming consumer minimal (repro on client side):

node-stream-client.js (node18+):
const fetch = require('node-fetch');
(async () => {
  const res = await fetch('https://local-rw:8443/v1/streams?model=test-sse', {agent: new (require('https').Agent)({rejectUnauthorized:false})});
  const reader = res.body.getReader();
  while (true) {
    const {value, done} = await reader.read();
    if (done) { console.log('done'); break; }
    process.stdout.write(value);
  }
})();

This precisely shows initial bytes then reader.read() hangs (not returning) during incidents.

3) Small Python SSE client (aiohttp) — helpful to reproduce ack timing differences:

python-sse-client.py:
import aiohttp, asyncio
async def main():
  async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as s:
    async with s.get('https://local-rw:8443/v1/streams?model=test-sse', ssl=False) as r:
      async for line in r.content:
        print(line)
asyncio.run(main())

4) Socat/netcat to simulate slow-client and force backpressure:

# open a TCP pair and relay slowly to simulate poor client's read speed
mkfifo /tmp/in /tmp/out
socat -v TCP-LISTEN:9001,reuseaddr,fork SYSTEM:"pv -qL 5 /tmp/out > /dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/8443" &
# curl to the sse endpoint but via the relay
curl -v --no-buffer http://127.0.0.1:9001/v1/streams?model=test-sse

pv -qL 5 throttles bytes to 5B/s which provokes send-buffer fill behavior quickly; good to reproduce the stall.

5) Captures and kernel traces collected during a hang:
- tcpdump -i eth0 -s 0 -w /tmp/hang-20260305.pcap host 10.0.2.5 and port 8443
- strace -p <server-pid> -e trace=write -ttt -o /tmp/strace-writes.log
- ss -tin sport = :8443 (check send-q)
- sudo grep . /proc/net/tcp | awk '{print $2, $3, $4, $5}' to inspect buffers and retransmits

Snippet I copied from strace during one hang (trimmed):
write(45, "4\r\n{\"data\":\"...\"}\r\n", 20)
write(45, "0\r\n\r\n", 5)
write(45, "\", 0) = 0

The zero-length write above is suspicious — indicates a non-blocking write loop that attempts a write of 0 bytes and returns which then trips into a wait path. Need to instrument writer to log when trying to send empty buffers.

6) Inspecting raw chunked frames (from tcpdump / Wireshark) showed sequences like: (hex of size) "0d\r\n{...}\r\n" then long pause then next chunk. For TLS traces, TLS records were sized ~16KB (typical) and we see one TLS record with partial JSON and then nothing.

Quick experiments that changed behavior:
- Adding header "Connection: keep-alive" didn't help.
- Turning off TLS (plain HTTP) reduced frequency (suggests TLS cycling).
- Adding nginx header X-Accel-Buffering: no reduced but didn't remove stalls (so not purely proxy buffering).
- Forcing TCP_NODELAY on client (curl --no-buffer implies it) made stalls less likely.

Actionable investigation steps (next):
1) Add debug logging in writer path to log: len(buf), attemptedWriteLen, returnedWriteErr, whether flush() called on TLS writer, and whether TLS.Write returned partial write. Timestamp each call (µs resolution).
2) Add instrumentation to runtime to track: bytesBufferedPerConn, TLSRecordBoundaryEvents, lastFlushTimestamp for each writer.
3) Reproduce with a test harness that isolates components: a minimal server that uses same TLS stack + SSE encoder but replaces model output with a deterministic stream with controlled pauses. If minimal server hangs, it points to TLS/libc/OS interaction. If not, it points to model/runtime path.

Minimal Go server (for isolation):
package main
import (
  "crypto/tls"
  "fmt"
  "net/http"
  "time"
)
func handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
  w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
  w.WriteHeader(200)
  for i:=0;i<200;i++{
    fmt.Fprintf(w, "data: chunk %d\n\n", i)
    if f, ok := w.(http.Flusher); ok { f.Flush() }
    time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)
  }
}
func main(){
  srv := &http.Server{Addr:":8443", TLSConfig: &tls.Config{MinVersion:tls.VersionTLS12}}
  http.HandleFunc("/sse", handler)
  srv.ListenAndServeTLS("cert.pem","key.pem")
}

Try running above with Go 1.20 and see if hang reproduces under same network throttle. If it does: capture strace and compare with production binary.

Logs & snippets to grab for ticket (INF-987):
- Full strace -e trace=write during hang
- tcpdump pcap and Wireshark export of TLS/TCP sequences around the stall
- runtime logs of bytesBufferedPerConn (add this)
- Minimal-server success/failure run artifacts and timings

Notes / stray ideas to test later:
- QUIC path: if clients use HTTP/3, check if similar stalls happen; QUIC framing differs so could isolate TLS/crypto vs transport issues.
- Check for TLS session resumption / renegotiation happening mid-stream (unlikely but check server logs).
- Validate server-side code never calls writer.Close() followed by extra writes (causes odd behavior).
- Reproduce with different Ciphersuites (turn off TLS13 or switch curve) to see if change in record sizes affects window.

Temporary mitigation for customers:
- Expose runtime knob to force smaller TLS record sizes (lower MSS-like behavior) or force TCP_NODELAY immediately before SSE writes.
- Document recommendation: set X-Accel-Buffering: no on proxies and ensure proxies forward chunked transfer as-is (no buffering).

Next steps for me:
- Add writer-level debug logs + enable in canary environment (start with 2% traffic).
- Run the Go minimal server under identical kernel settings and reproduce; attach to profiler/strace.
- Sync with Maya/Samir on kernel tcp settings we used in lab (we suspected tcp_autocork and tcp_mtu_probing earlier).
- If instrumentation points to TLS partial-write semantics, open GH PR to add defensive flush/looping logic when TLS Write returns short write (and log).

Open questions to discuss in triage:
- Is there any backoff logic in the runtime that could delay flushing after a partial write?
- Do we have any prior issues where model-side blocking (KV cache, disk) blocked the writer goroutine?
- Is nginx/ALB performing any transformation on chunk boundaries that we should blacklist for SSE endpoints?

Endnotes: keeping this as a personal scratchpad; will transfer findings to INF-987 ticket and attach pcaps/strace logs. If anyone reproduces quickly, paste timing of: first byte -> last byte before stall (ms) and number of bytes emitted.
